utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Yesterday evening, Ms. Pilipovic, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we discussed for one minute a possible very short extension of the cross-examination. Is it your wish to put any additional question after having put the case to the witness Mr. Henneberry?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. We would like to do it, with your leave - although we would have to clarify - that before the witness arrives, the Defence would like to bring up a point. We believe that we have to do this in closed session considering all the implications that could arise, and therefore, it would be appropriate for this to be done before the witness comes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...before we conclude the examination of this witness or -- I mean, is it related to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This has to do with the request or the motion from the Prosecution with regard to the new witness called AD, but I believe we have to do it immediately because the Defence needs to respect a certain notice and we would also like to ask your Chamber to reach a decision very quickly, which is why we would like to do this now, at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...for a while, Mr. Ierace, unless there would be any observation from your side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The only observation I would make, Mr. President, is that perhaps it would be more convenient for us to finish with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course. I am afraid we -- Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that we can't, or of course I do not know what you are going to -- what issue you are going to raise. But we might not be in a position to interrupt. So if it would be done before the first break, would that be sufficient for you or...?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as far as I am concerned, it will all be good enough for me. I don't know whether it would be good enough for your Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And since the CS disappears from my screen, please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would first of all like to thank the Prosecution since they reminded us of the Rule 90(H), but what happened yesterday with the witness yesterday is exemplary of the difficulties that the Defence has or can encounter during the cross-examination of some witnesses. First of all, this is with regard to the certain declarations that may have been given by General Galic. Obviously, with regard to the Articles 20 and 21 of the Statute, General Galic has a right to keep silence and does not have to testify unless he decides to. Now, if we say that General Galic never spoke and he does not have to testify against himself. Now, if the Defence lawyer within the privilege that he has with his client and that he has with the 87 of the Rules, perhaps it will not be possible, since this is his obligation, the Defence lawyers, to speak about it in the Chamber with regards to the cross-examination of a witness because of the privilege. Now, with regards to the Rule 90(H), it is true, Mr. Ierace, that the Rule has it that normally we would have to contradict the witness on each point that we want to bring up, but there are certain exceptions. First of all, there is the absolute right of the accused to keep silent and not to testify against himself and, therefore, the Defence lawyer has got an obligation to keep his secret. Now, perhaps it would be necessary, Mr. President, to explain this in relation to Rule 90(H), and we believe that here we have a case which is quite clear theoretically and in practice. There are certain questions that I will be able to ask the witness, and I thank you for it, and there are some questions that for once formulated in a rather vague way so that everybody would understand why am I choosing to formulate them in such a way, because I am trying to find the best way to respect the form and the substance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, my friend essentially is re-arguing whether indeed Rule 90 applies. He is subject to an interim order, and whatever view he has as to its appropriateness, the simple fact is that it does apply to him. What is required of him should take no more than 30 seconds. That is, if his instructions are that General Galic did not say what this witness says the General said, then he must simply put it to this witness that the General did not say those words or words like it. What is required is nothing more than that in relation to the evidence as it touches on General Galic. So far, my learned colleague has tested the reliability of the witness in relation to those conversations, as he is entitled to do. But to test the reliability of a witness is not the same as putting to a witness that the conversation didn't happen. One can test the reliability properly and still at a later point concede that the conversation happened. This is a matter which is well within the knowledge of General Galic. He knows either it was said or it wasn't. It seems on my reading of what my learned colleague has just said that he has in mind to ask a number of further questions of this witness. I could be mistaken, but if that is his intention, then, in my respectful submission, that should not happen. What simply remains at this stage is that the Defence be afforded the opportunity, if they want it, to put to the witness the parts of his evidence which are inconsistent with the Defence case. I note that during the cross-examination my learned colleague also challenged the witness's reliability in relation to his evidence in respect of Major Indjic. It may be that my friend is in a position, given his knowledge of the Defence case, to put certain things to the witness in relation to that evidence as well. It is a matter for him. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, as I told you yesterday, you may ask leave to the Chamber to put additional questions to the witness, very briefly, where if it is your intention to confront the witness with the Defence case, then you should put it to him and then you can ask questions about his earlier testimony which contradicts the Defence case. At the same time, you are fully entitled and your client is fully entitled to remain silent, but then there is no reason, in the view of this Chamber, to put any additional questions to the witness. I mean, you concluded the cross-examination yesterday. So if you would apply for leave to put such additional questions as to confront the witness with the Defence case, and you are under no obligation whatsoever to do so in this respect, we will fully respect this right of the Defence and of General Galic. But if you would decide that you would ask additional questions, then it should be after you have put the Defence case to the witness and then, of course, Rule 90(H) will apply. So it is up to the Defence on whether you want to further cross-examine, but only in this limited respect, the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I think there could be a middle way and I would just like to bring it up -- not to suggest it, but just to bring it up. One of the questions of the Defence -- one of the questions that the Defence would like to ask the witness and satisfy all sides is linked to his capacity to understand -- ability to understand the Serbian language and, therefore, many problems that could result from the fact that this witness only had a very limited knowledge of the Serbian language. So say that he was talking about this to General Galic and that he was not able to hear what General Galic said directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...response to this midway solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. My learned colleague's proposed line of questioning has absolutely nothing to do with Rule 90. And Rule Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 90 does not offend the right to silence. It does not oblige the accused to get into the witness box at any point. It is simply a requirement of the Rules in order -- which has the effect of clarifying the issues between the Prosecution and the Defence. More specifically, in relation to this line of questioning, yesterday my learned colleague asked the witness this question: "When you had meetings with General Galic, is it true to say that you were not able to speak directly with him because you do not speak Serbian?" Answer: "Yes." Question: "Therefore, you had to use an interpreter?" Answer: "Yes." And then later, "Who was the interpreter?" And then: "Most likely Jadranka," and so on. There were further questions about the interpreter. So for my learned colleague to now say that he wants to question the witness as to his understanding of Serbian clearly is illogical since, as he knows, the witness not only does not speak Serbian, didn't speak Serbian, but relied upon an interpreter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the Chamber has decided that it will maintain its decision. That means that if you -- well, at least, if you apply for leave to put further questions to the witness, that Rule 90(H) under (ii), especially the last part, should be applied. That means that your -- it was not a suggestion, but your idea on finding a midway solution is not accepted by the Chamber because what Mr. Ierace told us is true that yesterday it has been part of the cross-examination, part of the testimony of the witness, that he could not directly communicate, because of his lack of knowledge of the Serbian language, with General Galic. So, therefore, it is now up to you on whether you want to put very briefly your case where contradicted by the witness and ask him a limited number of questions or that you decide not to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I need time to confer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are just going to ask two questions, Mr. President, and I would like to thank you. We will be very brief. And General Galic will not disclose his case or, rather, he will not use his right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...you will put the case to him, or are these questions in respect of other issues? Well, of course, you -- we until now discussed an extension on the cross-examination on the basis of the observations made yesterday by Mr. Ierace. But I do understand that you now take a different line. You ask leave to put two short additional questions and you are not confronting the witness with the Defence case where he --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will confront the witness to his own statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no objection to my learned colleague asking some further questions in cross-examination, however, again it seems, if I understand my learned colleague correctly, that he is seeking to avoid Rule 90.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will not allow any circumvention of Rule 90(H) under (ii). Under this condition, the Chamber allows two additional questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, would you think it proper if it be explained for the benefit of General Galic the effect of it not being put to this witness, that his evidence, as it touches upon General Galic in particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, thank you very much for your assistance, and it is quite a new situation where the Prosecution seeks to protect the accused more or less. And it is not without hesitation, but let me just first ask a question, perhaps to General Galic. General Galic, I take it that since we had earlier discussions on Rule 90(H), that you fully understand what this Rule is about and that you also fully understand the consequences of not putting questions to the witness specifically on that part of his testimony where he tells the Chamber about meetings he had with you and the content of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you for giving me this time to give my opinion with regard to Rule 90(H). First of all, I would like to say that I am not very good in understanding the Rules, and I am not an expert and I have trouble in interpreting them. This is the first remark I have in response to your question. The second is that during the two years since the indictment was issued or, rather, the time of the indictment which is covered, the two years, there have been many discussions and many meetings and briefings, but the discussion of such nature and the declaration of such nature is illogical, is incompatible with my position, with the situation that I was in, and the political and military situation that the army of Republika Srpska was in. That is why I think that it can be concluded logically that in relation to that Rule and your question, Your Honours, that is all I would like to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then just try to explain, one of the risks of this situation might be: That if we are just talking about logics and if we are just talking about reliability, without putting the Defence case to the witness and ask him specific questions on meetings and the content of the meetings, later on, it could be understood as the testimony of the witness on these specific issues - I am talking about the meetings - whether they took place or not, the content of the meeting, was not contested by the Defence. That is, I think, the major issue. And of course, it is the Defence who finally decides what its position will be, what will be contested, what will not be contested, whether they will just want to limit the issue to whether it is logical, what the witness said, and not putting directly to him that either the meetings did not take place or that the content of the meetings was -- that the content of the discussions was not the content as it appears from the earlier testimony. If the Defence would need more time - I am not talking about days - but if you would like to have an adjournment for 10 minutes, the Chamber will gladly allow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we would like to have a five minute break, but we would like to indicate that the reasons for our determination is strategic since the Prosecution can also see what is at play. We would like to respect the right to silence, but you can see how much the -- how much the Rules 90(H) and 97 are in contradiction and how many problems we are having. We will need just five minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until 10.00. --- Break taken at 9.54 a.m. --- Upon resuming at 10.05 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving the Defence the opportunity to express itself, I would take the opportunity, first of all, to explain perhaps a bit more in detail Rule 90(H) under (i). Rule 90(H) under (i) says that, "Cross-examination shall be limited to the subject-matter of the evidence-in-chief and matters affecting the credibility of the witness and, where the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party, to the subject-matter of that case." It is only in respect of this last part of Rule 90(H), that is, if the cross-examination would go beyond the subject matter of the evidence in chief and does not concern the credibility of the witness, it is only to that last part that Rule 90(H)(ii) applies, that is, that the witness who is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party so that this is not on the subject of the evidence in chief or matters affecting the credibility, only then counsel shall put to that witness the nature of that case of the party for whom that counsel appears, and which contradicts the evidence given by the witness. Of course, this Chamber does not know what questions would be put to the witness by the Defence. And if there would be any reason that the Prosecution would think that it would be necessary in respect of a particular question that the case should be put to the witness, we will hear from the Prosecution. Of course, we cannot predict what questions you would put to the witness. The Defence will have an opportunity to put one or two questions, but they asked for two questions, two questions to the witness. But, of course, not those questions covered already by the cross-examination yesterday. Madam Registrar, would you -- let me just first ask: Is there any need, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, to put additional questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. There will be two or three additional questions in relation to Rule 90(H).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, 90(H). Under (i) or under (ii)? We will hear from that from you. Let's not try to guess and ask you to give information. We will hear your questions and then we will be in a position to decide. Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I only rise to my feet to seek the opportunity, not now, but at a later point and perhaps in writing, to respectfully put some submissions in relation to the interpretation by the Trial Chamber of 90(H)(ii). Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Madam Usher, [Realtime transcript read in error "Registrar"] would you please escort Mr. Henneberry into the courtroom. Just for the transcript, I was not asking Madam Registrar, but Madam Usher, to escort Mr. Henneberry into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, very briefly, I would just like to stress that there is a difficult -- difficulty that the lawyers note very well, which is the probatio diabolico since we are going to find ourselves in this case and I would like to draw attention to this. Thank you. For the transcript, probatio diabolico.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Henneberry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise that you had to wait for such a long time but procedural issues were asking our attention. Mr. Henneberry, I may - perhaps unnecessarily - but remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony. Before being re-examined by the Prosecution, there are not more than three questions to be put to you by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before we start, is there a volume control on this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is on the machine in front of you but Madam Usher will assist you. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Mr. Henneberry, bonjour.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bonjour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you very much for this. I appreciate. [Interpretation] I would just like to ask you to continue answering in French because that will be a lot easier for everyone. Now, sir, this is what I would like say: Now, the Defence contests resolutely not only the alleged meeting of the 16th of December, as well as anything that may have taken place at it, and I would like you to confirm clearly what you stated on the 2nd of July, 2000, in your witness statement, in your written statement that I have before me, and that I will read to you in a minute, and its reference number is 01008958. And I am going to now quote what you said so I am now going to go into English, with a pause. [In English] "I didn't have ready access to him since he was at a rank above which I would usually do." Full stop. [Interpretation] Sir, do you confirm that this is what you have stated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Two points, Mr. President. The transcript reads: "above which I would usually do." I think my friend meant to say, "above which I would usually deal," that is d-e-a-l. Secondly, my learned colleague asked the witness to read out this yesterday onto the transcript, which he did, so it is repetitive and lacks any relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is not in the transcript -- well, in the transcript, I see first part of a question. Is there anything else you would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Well, I would like to go ahead with the question, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, you stated in July 2000 that you did not have ready access to General Galic from the fact that you are at the rank below, and yesterday you stated that this didn't count for you. Wouldn't you here have to admit that on one of these two occasions, you did not tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I believe there was a misinterpretation or perhaps I didn't state clearly when I said that it didn't count for me. I stand by, "I didn't have ready access to General Galic." I also stand by the fact that I met several times with him. Generally, I would go through our liaison officer, Colonel Jakovic, or deal with most matters directly with the Corps Chief of Staff or operations officer. But I did meet with him several times. He was, however, not my first point of contact to deal with issues. I was to go through his staff and try to resolve them that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, since this meeting of the 16th of December is contested as having taken place, how come that since you took your time in looking over your statements and to modify some of them completely, that you cannot produce a single official document in order to prove that this meeting had taken place on the 16th of December?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: My learned colleague has put to the witness that he modified some of his statements, and once more, did so completely. I think, in my respectful submission, that can't be put. If my learned colleague thinks that, then he is obliged to take the witness to those modifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... a --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, gladly. We spoke about it at length yesterday. I asked the witness yesterday how come that in his statement from July 2000 he never mentioned the contents of the meeting that is being alleged today, the words that General Galic supposed to have added, and he almost miraculously produced them later, asked by I don't know whom. Now, these modifications obviously seem to be additional, and I believe that an addition is also a modification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's not lose ourselves in plays of words. Mr. Henneberry, is the question clear to you? The question is: Why -- what could explain that quite some new elements in your testimony in this court compared to what was in your original statement, original statement, the statement given before, what is the explanation of these new elements --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- coming up? Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with all due respect, that was not the question. The question was: Why there is no official document brought here to support this modification of statement of the witness. It is not why he changed the statement. He said that he looked over his documents, et cetera. But what I am saying is why there is not an official document which would establish this. Thank you, Mr. President. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I misrepresented your question, I fully agree with that, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. So that is the question. I was mainly concentrating on what was an addition. Let's talk about new elements. That is, I think, a fair representation of that part and why it is not supported by any official document or whatever document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand the question. So may I answer that then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason, sir, is there were no -- if you mean by an "official document" a transcript or something, we didn't keep notes or secretaries did not keep notes on the United Nations side for most of these meetings. The meetings were routine - not necessarily the meeting between General Galic and I - but there were several meetings and we had sometimes a dozen a day. I would like to add, sir, that my feelings and thoughts on the days were captured on notes like this. This single page represents seven days. That was my diary. So, I didn't put down everything. Some important details, as you call them, sir, such as when five of my colleagues were injured previously, that was becoming routine as well. You won't find that in a document but there are many medical records to back that up. That would be my response, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But, sir, the very last question, you, therefore, confirm that there is no document, no official document, in relation to -- either to the alleged meeting of the 16th December which is still contested by the Defence or in relation to the alleged words spoken by General Galic at the time of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only document would be my diary, sir, and you are correct, there is no official document on my part that would state the proceedings of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, could you please take one page of your diary. Could you just take it up.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...the diary?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Could you please just show it. This, sir, is the only element of any nature, either official or not, which would show that there was an alleged meeting of the 16th of December; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. There are United Nations documents, perhaps Colonel Mole's official documents and the agenda or reports by the senior military observer that may have those. I personally don't know of them, but I was not the only person at the meeting so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the sake of --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, the witness showed us a piece of paper which is approximately of the size of 10 centimetres by 5 centimetres, in which is filled by small handwriting. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Henneberry, you just said, "I was not the only person at the meeting." You also said in cross-examination that there was an interpreter present. I think you said his name was Jadranka. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jadranka, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How do you spell that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpreter Jadranka was Y-a-d-r-a-n as in "Nicholas" k-o. And if I may, sir, I believe I mentioned that I thought she was probably there as she was the normal one we used. I can't confirm positively that she was there

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would the last letter be an "A" or an "O"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An "A".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the transcript, it is "Jadranka" instead of "Jadranko."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The "Y," as well, sir, may be a "J," depending on the pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think you said that during cross-examination that she was of Serbian ethnicity. Was she -- who was she? Was she a United Nations interpreter or an interpreter for the SRK or who?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was a local person in the employ of the United Nations, as Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. most of the interpreters were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Had you experienced any problems with the quality of her interpreting on past occasions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If it wasn't her, then who else might it have been?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry that I have to intervene, for the reasons that you know already. This has to do with the transcript. I could see on several occasions that the French transcript does not carry the entirety of what is being said. For instance, here the half of the page has not been transcribed and I would like to -- I would like everything to be transcribed as accurately as possible. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Half of what page? I do not understand you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, gladly. It seems that half of the line which I just indicated which is now gone from my screen has not been translated into French, and this is not the first time. Page 6, line 17 -- 26, line 17, I believe. In any case, page 26, line 11, and then -- and then line 17 and 18 of page 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...read those parts not translated which would make it easier to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, gladly. Now, the first one, the first one we have is expressions "depending on the pronunciation," which has not been translated. This isn't very important. And then the second thing which was very important, this was the line 16, 17 and 18. I believe that the half sentence as most of the interpreters were -- was not translated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is line -- that is page 26, line 17, 18. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If it wasn't her that provided the interpretation on that occasion, who else might it have been?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It most likely would have been an interpreter working for General Galic and his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Coming back to that last answer that you gave in cross-examination, could you tell us who else was present apart from the people you have so far identified, that is yourself, Lieutenant Mole?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Mole, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: General Galic, one interpreter, perhaps Ms. Jadranko -- Ms. Jadranka. Who else?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was all, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, you were taken through certain passages in the redacted form of your diary that you provided to the OTP on the 2nd of October, 2000. Do you have a copy of that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have my original unredacted version. I don't have the redacted version with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could just check whether the page numbers correspond. Would you go to page 18?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have pages on this, sir. The date perhaps might -- the dates would correspond.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the witness be handed an unmarked copy of Exhibit P646. I have a copy at the bar table.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think you now have a copy of the relevant document. Would you please turn to page 18? The page number is indicated on the bottom left hand corner.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were asked to read certain passages from the entry for the 27th of November. Firstly, that, of course, is the 27th of November, 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You explained that passages made in italics were made by you after the original diary entry. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you make those comments at the time you constructed this redacted version of your diary, that is, for its forwarding in October 2000 or at an earlier time?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: At an earlier time, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you remember when it was that you made those comments which appear in italics?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: 9 November 1996. I say that because it is on my original copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, yesterday, you were asked or, rather, I should say certain words were read out from that entry, those words being: "Reports of 15.000 Muslim troops from Igman led by German including Leopard tanks." And then these words: "The hill overlooked most of the downtown area and whoever held it could bring fire to bear on the downtown." End quote. Do you remember that those words were put to you yesterday?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And then Mr. Piletta-Zanin said to you, "We are talking about the Olic hill." Do you remember that? Or "Zuc Olic hill," something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, that last sense appears in italics in this document, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And then underneath the paragraph in which that sentence appears, is there a further paragraph in italics?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do these words appear in that further paragraph, and I remind you of the earlier reference to reports of 15.000 Muslim troops from Igman lead by a German, including Leopard tanks. I will now quote the words from the following paragraph: "The report of a German commanding 15.000 troops plus Leopard tanks was never proven or disproved. Personally, I don't think it was true. The German supposedly commanding was said to have been an ex-colonel in the German army. However, the report of 15.000 troops on Mount Igman continued through to January. I believe there was some truth to the report because the Serb Corps made thorough and expensive preparations to repel a ground attack from Igman." Do those words appear?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. If you please go to page --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President. Just so that there is no problem in interpretation. I would like to ask my learned colleague if he can also give the commas and full stops so that there is no misunderstanding. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There don't seems to be any misunderstanding. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If you go over the page, certain words were read out from your entry for the 5th of December. The words which were read out were: "Front line destruction, tanks, vehicles, buildings, animals, people." Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, if you go to the beginning, first of all, for that entry, are the first words after "5 December," "Otes offensive Thursday, Muslims 500 killed in action." Do those words appear?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Beneath it, that is, beneath that paragraph, is there a paragraph in italics?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And in that paragraph, do you give something of an overview of what that report was all about?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In the last sentence of that paragraph, do these words appear: "This incident appears to have happened on Thursday, 3 December, but I didn't write it down until 5 December."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Coming back to the beginning of that italicised paragraph, do you explain that Otes was a small suburb of Sarajevo that had been held by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you say further that you "watched the battle from a hillside and thought it a classic ground battle except without the tanks."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is there, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you say these words: "I had never seen such a concentrated artillery and ground attack at that point. The outcome was that the Serbs took most of Otes"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise, but the French booth is asking me to slow down Mr. Ierace since they are having difficulties, it seems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, would you please slow down your speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And also could Mr. Ierace repeat his last question, the way it appears in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It appears in the transcript as I remember having heard it. And that was do you say these words --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think there are some words missing. THE COURT: Then please repeat you question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you say these words: "I had never seen such a concentrated artillery and ground attack to that point." Full stop. "The outcome was that the Serbs took most of Otes." Full stop.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, coming back to the words that were drawn to your attention in cross-examination, "Front line destruction, tanks, vehicles, buildings, animals, people," is that a reference to destruction on both sides of the confrontation line or the Bosnian government side or the Sarajevo Romanija Corps side?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is on the Bosnian government side. As we refer to it, the Muslim side, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Above it, the line above, do you say: "Went to L-3, watched Ilidza take hundreds of incoming burning civilian areas"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On what part of the confrontation line were those incoming received?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I apologise. I apologise. The interpretation in French is saying, "taking hundreds of civilian zones in flames." Now, I don't see the word "incoming." That has been omitted. This is incoming, is fire is what has been coming into the area. That has to appear in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You read the words literally, I take it, Mr. Ierace. Perhaps the witness could explain what "incoming" exactly means in this respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. I am just trying to find that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Second line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall that specific incident as I sit here, but the incoming to Ilidza refers to rounds landing on Ilidza, rounds that were fired by the Serb side on to the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification. Mr. Ierace, if there would be a suitable moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That is suitable, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an indication on how much time you would still need for the re-examination approximately?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No more than 10 minutes

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until 10 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, Ms. Pilipovic, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the issue you raised this morning in closed session, the Chamber expects that it can give a decision after the next break. Yes. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Henneberry, remaining on the same page, that is page 19, would you now please turn your attention to the entry for 7 December. These words were read out to you: "Heavy shelling in barracks. Multiple rocket launcher impacts. Muslims new weapons in area." Now, first of all, are there other words which appear in between the words which were read out?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was for 7 December, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry, I missed -- I can't seem to find that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Before the break, I took you to 5 December.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am on 7 December. I am just looking for your quote here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think the first words that appear alongside 7 December are "heavy shelling in barracks." Do you see those words?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And I think those words were drawn to your attention yesterday.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: After those words in italics, do these words appear: "Lukavica barracks HQ for UNMO L call signs and for the Sarajevo Romanija Corps"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Next words which appear after that are: "25 multiple rocket launcher impacts within 100 metre."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: "Buildings on fire, several wounded, seven killed."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, did you mean by that entry that there were 25 multiple rocket launcher impacts within an area of 100 metres or did you mean something else in relation to the reference to 100 meters?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant within 100 metres of my headquarters in Lukavica, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. It is extremely important in these questions. I am sorry to interrupt Mr. Ierace but it is very important that the interpretation is very precise. We are here talking about an impact of a multiple rocket launcher and it was not interpreted by the booth, and this is important because both army used it -- both armies used it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps if you slow down a bit, Mr. Ierace, we might have less problems. It does appear, however, from the answer that it was impact within 100 metres from the headquarters of the witness in Lukavica, which might explain something. But if you could just read that part which is not translated so that we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the current page, line 10, and the text says the following, [In English] that "There were 25 multiple rocket launcher impacts." This addition of multiple rocket launcher was not interpreted and that is important for the French transcript, for the reasons that you already know. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, this has been then corrected. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, I think your evidence is - please correct me if I am wrong - that your headquarters at Lukavica were in the same building as the office of General Galic. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Therefore, it follows that the rocket impacts were within 100 metres of the headquarters of the SRK. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Of the several wounded and seven killed, do you know how many were combatants?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Would you please now turn to page 26, in particular, an entry for 25 December. The last words on your diary entry were read out. Those words were: "Meeting Galic - Mole - I, boring," followed by three exclamation marks, "Airport road open."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Does that entry begin with the words: "Said goodbye to Mole"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Following the diary entry in italics, do you state: "This was Lieutenant-Colonel Mole's last day"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did the meeting with Galic and Mole have anything to do with the fact that it was Mole's last day?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was anything discussed beyond niceties to do with the fact that it was Mole's last day?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Mole expressed some frustration by way of a reminder to General Galic that the siege of Sarajevo - that may not have been the word he used, but that was the intent - was ongoing, that little progress had been made, that the shelling and activities continued. I believe General Galic again in a -- with some frustration on his part, restated his frustration with the Muslim forces and their activities towards Serbian civilians and whatnot.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember why it was that you used the word "boring" in your diary?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- the meeting was intended as a farewell. There was little of substance in the sense of both Colonel Mole and General Galic restating things that had already been said, and at that point, short of a significant incident such as the air corridor I mentioned previously, I felt that my job was out coordinating patrols, talking to brigades and whatnot. This particular meeting took me away from what I felt was my primary or most important function.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. The next entry is the 26th of December. On the second line, do these words appear, and also on the third line: "Need to brief Galic and local commander at L-2"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Having regard to the preceding words, was that proposed briefing of General Galic on your part in relation to the air operations agreement?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recollect whether that meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you remember when?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, would you please go to 4 August, which is on page five. These words were read out during cross-examination: "Muslim funeral shelled," and I pause to note that the word "Muslim" is in italics, " - news blames Serbs - I am not sure." And then do these words appear after that, firstly in brackets and italics: "(I have)," end italics, "much sympathy for common locals." Full stop. "Still objective." Full stop.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That appears, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And do those words reflect sympathy on your part for the locals in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those words reflect sympathy at that time primarily for the civilians and the innocents, as I called them, on the Serbian side. I had not yet been exposed much to the Bosnian or the Muslims inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do these words also appear in the same passage, being words that were read out yesterday: "Both sides continue shelling each other"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were asked questions about the shelling of the funeral and you said in response to those questions that -- firstly, there were strong indications or a strong probability that the Muslim forces had fired on their fellow citizens during a funeral. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You were asked whether that was a common thought by most UNMOs, and you said that it was. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether any investigation was carried out in relation to the shelling of any funerals which established that the source of fire was within the confrontation lines, that is, on the Bosnian government side?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Some investigations took place. In order to accurately determine where fire commenced from, one must conduct what is called a crater analysis, a scientific, a military, technological look at the impact ground. With respect to the funeral, I don't know that a crater analysis was done. I am aware that, as a minimum, an informal investigation was conducted by the United Nations, perhaps more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is that in relation to the incident on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Do you know whether any investigations were carried out in relation to the shelling of funerals at any other time with the finding that the shell had originated within the Bosnian government territory of the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speaking specifically to funerals, I don't recall. Other incidents were investigated. And I believe, for political reasons, no public categorical statement that the Muslims were shelling their own was made. However, it was, if I can use the term "common knowledge" that the investigations strongly pointed to the fact that the Muslim forces did, on occasion, shell their own civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to those investigations which strongly pointed to the shells having originated on the Bosnian government side, do you recollect the nature of the impact points?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specific areas are you enquiring about?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Not so much specific areas, but types of targets, if you have that recollection.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The marketplace and gathering points were common target areas, whether people were queueing for water, United Nations' aid, or buying what little there was available in the markets. Those were common areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you be more specific as to dates in relation to those targets?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you at least indicate whether any of those incidents that you have referred to occurred after mid-September 1992?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Going through those individually, you say: "People queueing for water." How many investigations are you aware of where the results strongly pointed to the shell or shells having originated on the Bosnian government side?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Off the top of my head, I can recall four that I believe stated that the shells were fired by the Bosnian Muslims on to their own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you assist us with where those water queues were?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the incidents I am talking about were generally inside, well inside, the city boundary of Sarajevo and well inside the known line of confrontation inside the -- excuse me -- the Muslim area. I cannot provide addresses at the moment. I simply have forgotten that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was your source of information in relation to these specific investigations, that is, where the shelling originated on the Bosnian government side?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source I believed most was the reports from the UN headquarters in the PTT and briefings that I attended on the UNMO side at the PTT routinely. They did make the news, the radio, that I heard, but very early on, I learned not to believe the news.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Who gave the briefings in the PTT?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was a United Nations briefing, it was usually given by the operation staff at UN -- at the UN level as opposed to the UNMO level. The operations staff would consist of intelligence and operations people. Specifically, I recall a French officer an operations person and a Canadian officer on the UNMO side. If it was a briefing internal to the UNMOs, it would be given by the senior military observer or his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, first of all, in relation to the briefings given by the operations staff, you say that you recall a French officer and a Canadian officer. What was the name of the French officer?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was the name of the Canadian officer?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've forgotten his first name, but it was Major Jackson, and his first name is somewhere in my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recall a time frame for, firstly, the French officer, that is, a period of time during which he gave these briefings?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that I was attending as a senior UNMO at that time, it would have been late fall, perhaps early winter, after sort of mid-October onward. Most likely in December.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you give us a time frame for Jackson, that is, the Canadian officer?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Earlier than that. I couldn't state a specific end date, but he was in Sarajevo when I arrived and was there for -- there until at least two months after. So I would estimate into October, and the briefings would have been a weekly briefing that I would have attended on only a couple of occasions in that time frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That is the time frame of about two months; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And I think you said that you arrived in July?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir. End of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. So we are talking effectively about the months of August and September; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, you said that you attended -- I am sorry, you said that the briefing on the UNMO side would be given by the senior military observer or his deputy?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Who was the senior military officer when you first arrived?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Grey from, I believe, the Australian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of his deputy?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If not immediately, then certainly shortly after my arrival, his deputy was Major James De Rosenroll from the Canadian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could you please spell his first name?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: D -- correction: Small d-e, space, capital R-o-s-e-n as in "Nicholas" r-o-l. I believe there is a second "L" at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, when did Lieutenant-Colonel Grey leave that position?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within a week or two, perhaps three, after our arrival, I believe. At that time, I was a commander of a single site and was not used to the overall procedures yet. So I can't be more specific than that. It was shortly after our arrival, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was he then replaced by Lieutenant-Colonel Mole or someone else?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: By Lieutenant-Colonel Mole.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And Lieutenant-Colonel Mole was the senior military observer until the 25th of December, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Clearly any briefings, therefore, that were given by the senior military officer from mid-August until the 25th of December would have been given by him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir, or Major de Rosenroll as his deputy, but the senior officer was Colonel Mole.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Certainly, if they were given by his deputy, you would expect Lieutenant-Colonel Mole to be aware of them?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Mole was replaced by Cutler; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And was he the senior military observer until when you left?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, I think you said there were two sources of these briefings: One was the senior military observer or his deputy and the second was the operations staff of the UN in the PTT building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you expect the senior military observer to be aware of the content of briefings given by the operations staff?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Undoubtedly, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, if I understand your evidence correctly, it is that the most reliable information that you had to the effect that sites such as water queues or marketplaces or aid sites were shelled from sources within the confrontation lines were from these two types of briefings, both of which were held in the PTT building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. And did you understand that there were strong indications from investigations carried out on shellings of some of these sites that the source of fire was from within the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was frequently the case, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. You were also asked yesterday in cross-examination whether women were members of the ABiH, and you said that they were. In what roles did you observe women in the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't state that I knew their roles. I did see them in uniform amongst soldiers or relatively senior ABiH staff or people.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It is interesting that you say you saw them in uniform. You were there until February 1993. Can you tell us in what sort of places you saw women in uniform on the ABiH side?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The best way to describe the two that I can recall, one would be downtown in the vicinity of the Presidency building, generally milling about with other soldiers, and one was definitely on the road between Sarajevo and Rajlovac on the front line, on the Muslim side, with two to three other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you remember any other specific instances where you saw women in a situation which clearly communicated to you that they were within the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, not at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. On both of those occasions, they were in uniform, I think you said?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were also asked some questions about the significance of someone in the position of Major Indjic revealing to you information on a corps plan. You were asked if that would be a very important fact and you said: "Important for a number of reasons."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise but, again, the French interpretation is talking of a corps or, rather, should be talking about a corps plan since yesterday, if you remember, Mr. President, we were talking about an Army Corps plan. So this is just for the transcript. This is about what has just been said by my learned colleague, and I have a line before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that page 46, line 16, "information on a corps plan"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is right. The first part of line 16 of the current page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, just for practical purposes, if you would have said, "I am sorry, Mr. President, but line 46 -- page 46, line 16, a corps plan has not been translated into French," that would have easily been done. That is the quickest and shortest way of dealing with it. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What were those reasons?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The several reasons were that I knew up front from the first moment, based on training and experience, that as an intelligence officer, major -- then captain but later Major Indjic, was trying to develop me as a contact. He was going to try to use me. That is clear. That is what anyone should do. Perhaps he knew as well that I was going to do the same thing. Traditionally, intelligence officers will develop a contact, but I did not have an intelligence officer, so I had to do that myself. That is what I was attempting to do with Major Indjic. I also had to report back what he was telling me, and it would be corroborated or not with other information by the UN intelligence people at the PTT. If two or more sources corroborated what Major Indjic said, that would give him a certain reliability status as a contact, whereas, if his information was not corroborated or was wrong, it would tell us another thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to the specific information that he gave you, that it was a corps plan, did you have source of -- withdraw that. Did you, in fact, have corroboration?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say, "I had corroboration," that was corroborated by the intelligence and operations people in the PTT and then the UN intelligence and operations people in the PTT, and that information that there was a plan was relayed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was the nature of the corroborative material?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. It would then have been other sources and good intelligence people won't reveal all of their sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recollect the names of those intelligence and operations people? I am not asking you to state them in open court, but do you recollect them?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Other than Major Jackson was probably one of them as a senior operations person, but specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are there any other reasons that you had in mind when you said that there are a number of reasons?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because if Major Indjic turned out to be a reliable contact, his information could streamline certain issues, could save UN or other lives, and perhaps as importantly, if he was giving me reliable information, he would be expecting something in return. And I would have to then determine how much information I could give him in order to maintain the open relationship or, in essence, maintain him as a contact, to use him, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Henneberry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That concludes re-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace. It was a bit more than 10 minutes, but I think it was not unfair to the Defence to allow you to continue. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, according to the Rule, there are certain new points that have been raised by Mr. Ierace and the Defence is applying for leave to your Chamber to ask some brief questions with regards to these new points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, thank you again. The Prosecution asked you certain questions about Ilidza and you were asked about some questions about acts in Ilidza. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: What acts in Ilidza? Sir, I don't recall the name Ilidza. Are you talking the funeral, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am sorry, I am talking about Ilidza. I am talking about Ilidza. Could you tell us, please, which side was in control of that part of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the main, it was the Muslim side, but I would have to see a map to make a better determination. It may have been totally in their control, but I would have to see a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, if you are not certain, you would not exclude the possibility that a large part of that territory was in Serbian hands?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without looking at a map, you are right, sir, I cannot state that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you were asked about a meeting which allegedly took place on the 25th of December. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, who according to you, would have -- and this is a conditional: Who would have attended this meeting apart from the persons that you told us about?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would have been an interpreter as well, and that was most likely all. So a total of four.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Including yourself?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And who would have been the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either Jadranka of our employ or an interpreter of General Galic's. Perhaps both, but I simply don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: It is, however, true that we can consider that you do not recall this?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpreters? That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, earlier, you were asked about the shellings that took place in Sarajevo and your statement was quoted recalling the following elements, [In English] "Confrontation lines." May I ask you to clarify that your statement -- in your statement it said that it was possible that the Bosnian government troops did fire at their own people?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Your question is not complete, sir, but, yes, that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. [In English] I know that sometimes we do have some difficulties with the transcript. Thank you for that. But I cannot read it and try to ask my questions. I am quite sure you will understand it.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much for that. I will go ahead in French. [Interpretation] Sir, when we are talking about the shelling, is it possible, as far as you can recall, that the shellings, that the responsibility would come from the Muslim side for their own people, would it have occurred in the area known as Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may just delay here, I am picturing in my mind the various places. But in fact Dobrinja is very clear now and, yes, that was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am just reminding you so that things are clear, Dobrinja is the neighbouring area to the landing strip of the airport, it is to the north of the airport. Is that what you remember, sir?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it being beside, immediately beside the airport, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, is it possible that such shelling also occurred in the area known as Alipasino Polje? I am reminding you that this is a neighbourhood which is a little to the north of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It is possible that that could have happened anywhere in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I would like to go back to your information sources or your intelligence sources. When you spoke of a corps plan, did I understand it correctly sir, your testimony purports that you could not give any name of any officers, intelligence officers, who would have confirmed the alleged existence of a corps plan which is contested by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for your answer. I would like to go back to Major Indjic now. Do you remember when you spoke to him, generally speaking, not the dates, but time of the day?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: From first thing in the morning, being 7.00 a.m., through to midnight, we spoke frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this question, it seems to go in one sense well beyond re-examination, but in another sense seems to relate to nothing that was asked in re-examination or any answers that were given in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you please indicate where this issue has been raised in the re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Earlier, Mr. Ierace mentioned the name of Mr. Indjic, of Major Indjic. He was quoted on several occasions, and it seems that Major Indjic would have been the only source that this witness can indicate as being relative to the alleged existence of a corps plan. Now, the reason why I want to ask this question is in relation to the additional questions by the Prosecution, as well as with regard to the circumstances, personal circumstances, with regard to Major Indjic, and I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. believe that the Defence is authorised to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It might not have been a totally new issue, but is my recollection correct, Mr. Ierace, when you asked some questions about the relationship with Major Indjic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I didn't ask any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but it was part of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The only question I asked the witness was what the reasons were that he regarded, that is the witness regarded, Mr. Indjic's revelation of a corps plan as being important. And that flowed directly from a question asked in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then, of course, part of the testimony was about the way the witness communicated and behaved in respect of Major Indjic. One question you are allowed to put.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
