utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: It is a -- all the more simple question because it is a fact. It is true, and I believe it comes from your statement and your testimony, is it true to say that Major Indjic had a serious drinking problem?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That is something that could have easily been put in cross-examination and it certainly doesn't arise from re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree with you. We will allow one question since part of the testimony was, although not specifically asked, was about Major Indjic. But there is no reason whatsoever why you would not have put this question in cross-examination, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. So I gave you an opportunity to put one question and I would say that was intended to take advantage of the possibility given, and I might remind this for future situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the question stands and the answer stands --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- had it been asked in cross-examination, it would have been a subject of re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I will given you an opportunity to re-examine the witness in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise. I hope that you will accept my apologies. It is not manipulation on my part, but simply in good faith, I thought that I would be authorised to ask this question. Very well. I will not ask it. I will ask other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've asked it; it has been answered. Mr. Ierace will get an opportunity to re-examine the witness on this issue. Please proceed

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very last question, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very last question, sir. Does the name or the abbreviation of Sib, S-i-b- or C-i-b, mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. Perhaps my friend can explain how this arises from re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This means that you withdraw the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if I am told no, then I won't ask it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't remember that I said no, but I just wanted to make clear to you that if you would start to explain in the presence of the witness, the relevance of the question what it was about, et cetera et cetera, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is very simple, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I would just like to see where in the re-examination it appears that the Prosecution has asked any questions about Sib or that it was part of the testimony, even if not specifically, asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. In a few words, in a nutshell, it is perhaps a problem of interpretation that we would like to clarify. We spoke of a meeting of the 25th of December, and I think that it was in 1992, when this meeting took place with General Mole -- or Colonel Mole, and it seems that in some translations that we have here we are talking about Sib. Now I wanted just to make it clear, since we do not know who the translator is, I just want to find out who was there. So now this is not a vital question for the trial and, of course, we don't have to ask it. It is not going to change anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mr. Ierace, I promised that I would give you an opportunity to re-examine the witness on the specific issue of any, I think, alcohol abuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Henneberry, you were asked whether it was the case that Major Indjic had a serious drinking problem, and you said that he did. First of all, as a cultural characteristic, in your experience, when dealing with members of the Serb community, especially man to man, was it the case from time to time that alcohol was taken?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was there a particular drink that was favoured by members of the Serb community on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slivovitz, sir, and please don't ask me to spell that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Okay. How common was that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was almost always a way of commencing a meeting and was available during meetings and of ending meetings with Serb military.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether declining to join, on the part of yourself or someone else in your position, was undesirable or desirable? In other words, was there any expectation as a matter of culture, if you like, that people would do this, would partake?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, declining to partake, it was commonly thought that that was an affront or an insult to the Serbs, but I personal know that thought was a myth. After about a month or six weeks, I simply didn't drink and it did not hinder my relationship with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, during your many meetings, I think you have told us at least hundreds of meetings with Major Indjic, did he consume alcohol in some of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did he consume alcohol during all of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you give us an approximation in terms of a percentage as to during how many of those meetings he consumed alcohol?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately a third. So 33 per cent, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to the remaining two-thirds, on any of those meetings, did he seem to you to be under the effects of alcohol?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you give me an approximation in terms of percentages of how many of those meetings, that is the two-thirds, he appeared to you to be under the effects of alcohol?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be very few, a minuscule per cent, that he appeared to be under the effects, but there would be some occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, the issue of alcohol has been raised in the context of your evidence as to the revelation by Major Indjic of indiscriminate fire being part of the corps plan. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Two possible ways --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am objecting to this because I think that we are going now to another side. We are slipping to an abyss of the other side of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do press this question and this line of questioning. The issue has been raised by the Defence and I must respond to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the objection is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Henneberry, there are two possible ways, perhaps there are more, in which a serious drinking problem on the part of Major Indjic may be relevant to your evidence of his revelation to you of the existence of the plan. One way is that it may, in part or in whole, be the subject of a fantasy, alcohol-induced. Another way is that it may have loosened his lips but what he said is reliable. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the first hypothesis, was there anything about what he said or the way in which he said it which raised in your mind even a question that his confiding in you that indiscriminate fire was part of a corps plan was a fantasy?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was there anything about what he said or the way he said it which made you think that he was guilty of indiscretion and revealing to you something which perhaps he would not have done, had he been sober?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On how many of the occasions that he discussed this aspect of the corps plan with you was he, in your mind, drunk?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't even begin to think, sir. We had so many meetings and the topic was so frequent, I can't even guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. In terms of percentages, would you be able to give us some idea or not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Was there any occasion when he wasn't under the influence of alcohol that he spoke of this aspect of the corps plan?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was there anything he said to you -- on those occasions when he wasn't under the influence of alcohol, was there anything he said about the corps plan which was inconsistent with what he had told you when he was heavily under the influence?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Henneberry, Judge Nieto-Navia has one or more questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: First I would like to know, Mr. Ierace, if your intentions are to tender Exhibit 646.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President -- Your Honour - I'm sorry - I am happy to do so. I had been following the recent pattern of, where possible, not tendering material and instead relying on what was said by the witness or by counsel. But I see nothing improper in the Bench requesting that I tender something and then doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if I may guide the parties in this respect, that was a technique we used when only a small part of a large document would be presented to the witness, and in order to avoid any contamination and in order to keep the pile of paper within certain limits, we -- that is what we suggested to the parties. But I think the Chamber has got a feeling that we have no context any more now major parts of this document have been presented to the witness in italics -- not in italics, line before, line afterwards. So that is the reason perhaps why, under these circumstances, it would have been better to produce the document. Of course, in the beginning, we could not guess to what extent the document would be quoted. But I think we heard approximately a quarter of it by now. And the next time, if there is a similar approach, I think we -- it is not isolated parts of the document any more, it is the general part of the document that has been presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just in relation to that, the practice that I have adopted and which I propose to continue, is to place the relevant documents on the exhibit list, in other words, the documents which the Prosecution proposes to tender, and if there is only a line, to avoid the unnecessary handling of paper and not tender them, but I remain quite open to a request from either the Bench --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must interrupt, Mr. Ierace, and I apologise because the French booth, whatever the reason is, is unable to follow you and they are protesting to me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, simply put, they will be on the exhibit list. If either the Defence or the Bench would prefer that a particular document is tendered, then because they are already on the exhibit list, they can easily be done. And with documents such as the redacted diary, we would -- given what you have just said, a document of that nature, we would in fact tender in the future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I was interrupting Judge Nieto-Navia. I am sorry, but I am afraid otherwise I would have forgotten to give you guidance on this. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If the document is going to be tendered, I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just El Mahdi has one or more questions to you as well. Or no questions. 13

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask for a clarification, please, and I was wondering whether you can help me to see things more clearly. In your opinion, as an officer, from the positions of the Serb army on the hills as you explained on the map, and the type of weaponry that existed, would it be possible for you to read a strategy in it from these positions independently of what you may have heard or not have heard? You as a military officer, from the type of weaponry and the positions, would you be able to read into it a kind of strategy, whether offensive or defensive, and the gamut of in between these two?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Given the placement of the weapons, the fact that weapons, additional weapons, were known to exist but we did not have access to them, and that additional weapons were moved in, combined with the overall lack of sufficient manpower, particularly front line soldiers, and the requirement for those soldiers elsewhere in Bosnia and the theatre, it was my speculation, although it seemed obvious to me, that the intent was to completely encircle the city to prevent supplies from moving in or out and to essentially wait out the Serb -- correction, the Serbs to essentially wait out the Muslims and/or starve them out, maintain complete control of the city to their advantage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In a sense of the type of weaponry, if you can just help us in this, what could you read into the type of weapons that were positioned in these emplacements?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. The first thing was that heavy weaponry, and by that I will talk about mortars and above, anti-aircraft weapons and whatnot, were in scarce supply on both sides. There was a significant mix of very old weapons and some newer modern weapons. So neither side had a modern military, so to speak. The weapons that the Serbian side had were capable of reaching anywhere in the city, either directly or indirectly -- correction, certainly indirectly, and most of the city with direct fire weapons. And they could be used, depending on the situation, in combination. For instance, indirect fire that would keep the heads down of any opposition while the -- in this case, the Serbian military could move forward, or direct fire, especially the large calibre weapons such as anti-aircraft weapons, were capable of terrorising those who were near its impact by its sheer nature of explosion and spread pattern of fragments, and the anti-aircraft weapons were capable of firing through buildings. So if the force, an opposition was believed to be inside a building, the anti-aircraft weapons could fire through the walls of the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would also like to ask you a question in relation to Lima 10 and Lima 11. You said that the shots, the fire, that came from these two positions, were mostly fired in order to cause terror. Why and how did you come to this conclusion? And why specifically these two positions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I believe what I meant to say was Lima 7 was fired primarily to invoke terror. Positions Lima 10 and 11 fired into the city as well and also on to the front line. I am sorry, I've forgotten the second part of your question. If I may read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How were you able to come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they were hitting, frequently hitting from those two specific positions, hitting civilian areas inside the city, and I could know that by the reports coming from my colleagues inside the city. I would see a weapon fired, they would report an impact of the same calibre of weapon, and so they could be put together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we are talking here about position 7, or was it 10 and 11?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To clarify, Your Honour, position 7 had a domineering look at the city; it could see everything. Most of the firing from 7 was indiscriminate and fired into the city, that I could personally see the weapon fired and the impact. Position 10 and 11, I often could not see the impact and relied on my colleagues. However, the impacts that I could see from the weapons fired from positions 10 and 11 did occasionally hit homes and buildings known to have been occupied by civilians, or were fired in a manner that kept people running from building to building, "on their toes" is a phrase we use in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no interpretation into English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters. I am going to ask the question again, and I was asking for a clarification in relation to the weapons of the BH forces. During your period while you were there, there was talk of a lack of weapons, most of the time. Is it true that most men of military age, so to speak, were able to bear weapons, in effect, or was there a substantial shortage of weapons? What was your impression?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression on the BH side was that at least those on the front lines all had, in a military term, a "personal" weapon, meaning a rifle of some sort. Whether or not they had to exchange those when they left the position, I don't recall hearing that. Therefore, I would conclude today that all of the soldiers had a rifle of some sort. With regard to heavy weapons, again, mortars and anti-aircraft, there was a definite shortage on the BH side up until about December, when they started to re-equip or be re-equipped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you saw two women in military uniform, which suggests that they were members of the army. You spoke of two women. Were they bearing weapons?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least one was, sir. I don't recall the one by the Presidency. I would say probably. But definitely on the one on the road leading to Rajlovac had a weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in your opinion, was she going to the front line? Was she involved actively or was she perhaps working in the administrative services or other services?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw her on the front line, sir. She was on the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge El Mahdi. I have a few questions for you as well. Could perhaps first Exhibit P3449 be presented to the witness. These are the photographs. Mr. Henneberry, you have answered questions about two photographs that are taken, I would say, in the field. That is the first photograph that is, last four digits are 9095, and photograph with, in the right bottom corner, 92125, someone with a Canadian emblem on his uniform. Could you please look at the other picture that is also taken in the field which has at its back - perhaps you could look at the back - ERN number ending with 9090 in red.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that picture taken approximately from the same position as the other ones?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am asking you this -- well, let me first have the next question. Does it give a similar view at least of the area covered as part of the other pictures?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This view, I believe, sir, would be looking more from the south-west into the city. I would have to confirm with a map. Whereas the other two are almost due west. So there would be a difference in how much of the city was exposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I am asking you specifically about a small, square relatively light rectangle in the lower-left part which has the appearance of a building at a distance. I don't know whether it is a building or not. And on the relatively unwooded area on the hill in front, would this structure in this area with hardly any trees, the part where there is no bush and no trees, on the right upper side of this hill, would that be the same on the three pictures because I see a similar structure and a similar area with hardly any bush or wood?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It appears to be the same. The building and the open area is the same. The view is slightly different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would that mean that if the view would be clear, that you would see from those positions as appear in the two other photographs with people on it, would be approximately the same as in that third photograph with no people on it? I mean the view on the city, especially distance, buildings.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Henneberry, you have been confronted with document D108, which starts with: "You will no doubt be aware of the incident at Lima 7 on the 19th of December 1992." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you just give us a brief indication, not more than that at this very moment, of what was the incident at Lima 7 on the 19th of December?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a perceived hostage-taking of UNMOs by Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your answer. I noted that on the map we looked at Lima 7 is indicated in a slightly different way compared to all the other positions, that is that the small circle next to it is white, where all the others are black. Has this a specific meaning?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect it is just a technical matter, sir. I don't recall off the top of my head. As in the difference between the black and white circle, Lima 7, the position was different, but on the map, if I could see the map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could perhaps Exhibit P742 be shown to the witness again. You said the difference --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I can state with some confidence that that was just a matter of the machine used to reproduce the map and it was a technical one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. You testified about shelling targeting within the boundaries of the city, shelling people from the ABiH population by ABiH forces. How frequent was that? Could you give us a further indication.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speculatively, it was relatively frequent, especially when the press were around. I say, "speculatively" because not all incidents were investigated. But there was a direct correlation to when the press were visiting the ABiH positions or forces to the number of shells or the frequency of shelling inside the city. So I suspect that those shells, those incidents, were generally done by the ABiH forces, and that was a common feeling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You are talking about several specific types of targets. You mentioned markets.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us a better indication of markets. We heard a lot of testimony - you will not be surprised - about one market. Would that market be included in your assessment or would it not; it would be the Markale market?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- I wasn't considering that one, sir. That happened after I had gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you indicate what other markets you were considering?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the first few months when I was there, there was very, very little to buy inside and outside the city. Whenever a shipment would come in of whatever, food, UN aid, even that was being resold, an impromptu market would open up or perhaps it would be taken to a former thriving marketplace and then put on display. They weren't permanent markets in the sense they were open all the time. They were just gathering places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. Was this phenomena which you would described as being relatively frequent reported to the ABiH headquarters -- was there any complaint? This Chamber has heard testimony -- not testimony, but has seen evidence, whether it was complained about, using hospital grounds for firing mortars. Are there similar complaints, either in writing or recorded in whatever other way, to the ABiH forces complaining about this shelling their own civilian population?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am told that there are, and I believe that there are. Not by me because I would have had nothing to do with that. But I am almost certain that there are and I also know that the response was often by the ABiH Presidency diplomats that the UN had no right to accuse them of shelling their own people, that the Serbs were the aggressors. In essence, they denied that they were doing it by trying to deflect the blame to the Serbs

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is the source of the knowledge of these replies?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefings, reports and discussions of the PTT headquarters of the UN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last question: Would it be able, in your view, to retrieve the reports of your discussions with General Galic and Major Indjic, especially in respect of the corps plan or destroying the city, getting rid of the Muslims, could be retrieved in any of the daily reports either made by your reports or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe in the official daily report, there would be mention of that. Especially, I understand there were two types of reports. One was generally unclassified. It went to New York over an unclassified means. There were other classified reports that spoke of delicate matters that emanated from the headquarters and they should be available. I can't imagine why they wouldn't be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much for your answers. This concludes your testimony, Mr. Henneberry. I see Mr. Piletta-Zanin --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. President, thank you. The Defence would like -- following one of the new points that were raised by your Chamber, the Defence would like to ask one -- only one question and this is the question asked by Judge El Mahdi in relation to reading of a military strategy in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you remember the question that you were asked by Judge El Mahdi earlier in relation to the possibility of being able to read a military strategy by you as a military person, military officer? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The question is the following: Would you be able to tell us, if you knew precisely two elements, firstly, the confrontation and separation lines between Bosnian Serbs on one side and BH army on the other side and, secondly, a different military installations and facilities in the city itself?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK HENNEBERRY [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to the confrontation line, my answer is yes, I knew what it was. With regard to all of the presumably ABiH military positions inside the city, I did not know of those until November or December. I was not permitted to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Henneberry, I was a bit too quick when I said that that was the end of your testimony in this courtroom. You also answered the last question from the Defence. You have answered a lot of questions from both parties during a long examination. You have also answered the questions of the Bench. I thank you very much for coming. It is important for us to hear the answers from those who have been present at the relevant times and the relevant places. Thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are welcome, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam usher, would you please -- well, we don't have to escort you out of the courtroom specifically. We will adjourn until 1.00 and then we will deal with the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 1.05 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Madam Registrar, may I ask your guidance in going through the documents that have been used during the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this juncture, I might formally indicate that I seek to tender Exhibit P646, which is the redacted diary and other documents prepared by the witness. Copies of that have been given to Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a document that we read from. This is complete. We object to this, and the reason is, Mr. President, is that we read certainly about 40 or so sentences from this document but the document contains a number of other information and there was no testimony on these other elements. Therefore, and following in the sense what was proposed at the time by the Prosecution, we had prepared ourselves for the reading of the documents, respecting the procedure so far. We cannot now be told one day something is being tendered and the next day that it is not being tendered. This time, we are objecting to the tendering of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, the Prosecution has throughout reserved its right to tender documents of which it gives notice in compliance with the seven-day rule, and this document comes within that ambit. At no stage has the Prosecution said that it definitely would not tender any of the documents of which the Defence has had notice in respect of this witness. Rather, as I explained earlier and as I have explained on other occasions to the Defence, we place on the sheet what we may tender and then see if we can avoid tendering by bringing out the relevant lines. So it is not, in my respectful submission, correct to say that the Defence has been mislead. The second issue that my friend raises is one of relevance, so it seems, that is, the fact that the document contains many passages which have not been made the subject of questioning. That alone is not a sufficient reason for the document not to be tendered. The witness was cross-examined at length about the sources of the material in the document, the reliability of the material in the document, and indeed he was cross-examined about the letter which accompanies the document when he forwarded it to the OTP on the 2nd of October, 2000. It is a document in every sense of the witness, contemporaneously made in the -- to the degree that it contains his diary entries. Those entries which were not contemporaneous are clearly indicated by italics. I press the tender. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As the parties may have noticed that the Chamber was very much interested to know whether the parties would tender the document or not because otherwise the Chamber might have asked for the production of this document and asked for it by itself. As I explained before, the practice used in this court - and I also explained the reasons why - is functioning quite well if you are dealing with an isolated part of a document, if the Chamber is in a position to have some idea of the context. But if we concentrate on a specific part of a document, it is also that we have some difficulties in understanding the context, was also due to the very fragmentaric use of document, where large portions of the document were read out. Sometimes the next line was not read out or the previous line, which created the feeling within the Chamber we would have to see the document in its whole and, therefore, the objection against the admission to evidence is denied. And this document, P646 is admitted into evidence. Madam Registrar, could you please guide us as far as the other documents are concerned. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Just so that I know, is this document going to be admitted as it is or is it going to be admitted as we have seen it on occasions, only with the relevant parts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...as a whole. And of course, as professional judges, we will take proper care that we use it in relation with the testimony given in this court. We have the testimony in our minds and in the transcript. But the document as such is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3705, diagram drawn by witness; Exhibit P3449, a set of five photographs; Exhibit P742, map; Exhibit P3644.PH, map marked by witness; Exhibit D108, UNPROFOR memo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All these documents are admitted into evidence. Then, Mr. Ierace, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The next witness is Edin Husovic, who will be taken by Prashanthe Mahindaratne, who is a member of the legal trial team, and present in court as well will be Daryl Mundis. And might I be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Mahindaratne, I might have some difficulties in pronouncing your name now and then but I hope you will accept apologies for that. Mr. Usher, could you please escort into the courtroom, Mr. Husovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear that you are responding in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that mean that you would like to give your testimony in English or in your native language? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It doesn't matter for me. I can speak English or Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is what you prefer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can speak in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can speak in English. If there would be any moment where you would prefer to use your own language, interpreters are there, so please inform the Chamber right away because we would like to avoid whatever confusion because of your mastering the language. Then, Mr. Husovic, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth at the beginning of your testimony. The text of this declaration will be handed out to you. If you would prefer to use your own language for your solemn declaration, please indicate so, because we have them available in both languages. Would you prefer the Bosnian-Serbian-Croat or the English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In English is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The usher hands out a text to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Bench and the Defence, this witness will be testifying with regard to shelling type incident number 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Husovic, would you please state your full name and spell out the last name?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Edin Husovic, and it is H-u-s-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Would you please state your date of birth and the town or municipality in which you were born?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on 27th of February, 1976.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did your family and yourself live in Sarajevo at any stage?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I would just like us to be very precise for technical reasons. Line 18, there is no French interpretation regarding the date of birth and the address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you please say when you lived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: I lived -- I was born and raised in Sarajevo. I have lived there from 1976 to 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, I have no interpretation. I don't know whether there is a problem, but there is no interpretation in French

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...keep a better --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether this is a technical reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The problem has been solved in the French booth. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Husovic, did you live in Sarajevo during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you please state what your occupation was during this period?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: I was just a student.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you regularly go to school or did the conflict affect your daily schooling?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it did. I was going to school, actually, in several apartments around my neighbourhood because we were not allowed to go to regular high school because they were bombing our neighbourhood occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Husovic, were you at any stage shot while you were living in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was shot by sniper on January 10th, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You recall that incident? How old were you when you were shot?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: I was 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you still a student then?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you specifically state the date and the time at which this incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: That was at January 10th, 1994, around 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What type of a day was this? Was it a clear day? Was there clear visibility?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: It was a clear and sunny day. It was clear visibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was it a calm day or was there much shooting during the course of the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I apologise. I think it is me, now. I can't follow and I am asking you to slow down because I would like to be able to see both transcripts at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It might be better that you just take a small pause after the witness has answered and that the witness takes a small pause after the question has been stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will repeat that question, Witness. Was it a calm day or was there much shooting during the course of the day?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: It was a very calm day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Where were you at the time? Can you describe the location at which you were?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: I was in the front of my building. There is a certain bar, pizzeria, and I was standing with a few friends of mine, just chatting, when shooting occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you please state the name of this area, the neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: It was on Cengic Vila and it is in front of Paradiso Pizzeria.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Paradiso Pizzeria was the restaurant you referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You referred to yourself being with friends. How many others were present with you at the time?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Five more guys.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you remember their names?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what the names were?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. It was Sead Kahrimanovic, Junuz Uzunovic, Mirsad Abdurahmanovic, Zijad Mujezinovic, and I can't remember the fifth one. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You did refer to Abdurahmanovic being present?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What were their occupations at the time?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: They were just civilians. They were unemployed at the time. They were just trying to survive, like everybody in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you remember the attire you were wearing at the time? You can just describe it only if you remember.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: I was wearing that -- it was jeans, tennis shoes, sweater and a jacket which was a kind of blue colour with white stripes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you remember what type of clothes your companions were wearing?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah. They were wearing jeans and just sport outfits.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that you and your friends were all in civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you or any one of your companions carrying any weapons or anything that resembled a weapon?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At the time, what were you and your companions doing?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: We were just standing, talking, chatting, telling each other jokes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you please describe the incident to us, the shooting incident?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: While, we were talking, I just heard a whistle, a bullet whistle, and a felt a huge pain in my abdominal area, fell on the ground, and two of my friends, they picked me up. They pulled me into Paradiso, into that pizzeria. I couldn't breathe. I couldn't see any holes on my jacket. I pulled my jacket and I saw red circle on my stomach. There was no blood. One of my friends -- actually, it was Mirsad Abdurahmanovic, he asked me if I am okay. I couldn't breathe. There was like maybe 20 more shots, shot at the time, so bullets were whistling still around that area. They just put me in a car and they drove me to the hospital. Sead Kahriman was driving at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You said you were taken to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 85.1, some 20 shots.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Who drove you to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: It was Sead Kahriman.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did anyone else accompany you to the hospital, apart from the person who drove the car?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: It was only Sead, but the other guys, they drove another car, so they were following us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: As a result of this shooting, were you injured?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was injured. My liver was damaged. I lost a lot of blood. I almost died.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Husovic, would you be able to say from which direction the shots came, from which direction you were fired at?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: They came from Hrasno Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you say Hrasno Brdo, what exactly do you mean? Can you briefly describe Hrasno Brdo to the Bench?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: That mountain it was located south from the pizzeria about maybe 1500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know which part to the conflict or which army controlled Hrasno Brdo?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Serbian part. Serbs, they controlled that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you be more specific when you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 85.24, I believe that I heard the witness speak of a mountain. In any case, I found it in the French interpretation, although it doesn't appear in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Husovic, it is my recollection that you talked about a hill, south from the pizzeria, maybe about 1500 metres from that. That was your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that it was a hill does not appear in the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. It was hill. Apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- transcript. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you refer to Serbs, who did you exactly refer to? Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Serbian army, probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the term VRS?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Vojska Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Who did you refer to when you said "Serbian army"?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Would you be able to recall as to which direction you were facing when you were shot?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: I was facing that hill, the Hrasno hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were the hills of Hrasno Brdo visible from where you were?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Husovic, did you see any military equipment or big military vehicles in the near vicinity at the location you were standing at when you were shot?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were there any military buildings or uniformed personnel nearby?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see any persons, civilians or otherwise, who were armed at the time nearby when you were shot?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you specifically recall about how many shots you heard at the time?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: At least 20 shots. I am sorry, I really didn't count at the time. I was still in shock.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You said you were taken to hospital for treatment for the injuries you sustained in this shooting incident?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you remember how long you were in hospital?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: I was in hospital 10 days, even though my treatment required more than 10 days. But it was not that many beds available.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you left the hospital, were you given a letter of discharge?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown Exhibit number 2097.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to take this opportunity to indicate on line 10 on the previous page that personnel in uniform, words "personnel in uniform" had not been interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the French transcript or --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: "Uniformed personnel" into the French transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, "uniformed personnel." Please proceed Ms. Mahindaratne. You asked -- yes, we have the document in front of us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Husovic, do you recognise the document which was just shown to you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your name is included there?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is that your address which is included there?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your father's name is there?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is that the letter of discharge that was issued to you when you left hospital?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown Exhibit number 2114.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Husovic, are you aware that an official report was made of your -- the shooting incident you just testified about?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document which was just shown to you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is your full name indicated in that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is that the official report that was made with regard to the incident you just testified about?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown Exhibit number 3236.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, I have been informed that we should stop today at 1.45 sharp. So I don't know, if it is just one or two questions that you would like to put to the witness in respect of this new document, please proceed. If not, perhaps we could conclude for today. I will leave it up to you how to finish in the next two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just have a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you think you can do it in, let's say, two, three minutes, that is fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I should be able to do it. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Husovic, you gave two statements to an investigator from the Tribunal with regard to your shooting incident?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At the time you marked a particular map indicating the location you were standing at, at the time you were shot?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is that the map that was just shown to you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: On that map, you circled in red the building where the Paradiso restaurant was and marked it as number 1?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In that circle you also indicated with an "X" the position you were standing at, at the time you were shot?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You also circled in red the building in which a market was and marked it as number 2?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Chamber what this -- the Bench, what the market was when you refer to it as number 2?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: This right here was a marketplace where people would buy their food and they would trade food for cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was this market regularly patronised by civilians?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I have just one last question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but the French booth has not been able to understand. Perhaps if the penultimate question could be repeated, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was this market regularly patronised by civilians?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Bench as to who controlled the area where restaurant Paradiso was located, which party to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSOVIC
utterances.text: Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is all, Mr. President. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not for today or would this conclude the examination-in-chief as a whole?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This would conclude examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Mahindaratne. Mr. Husovic, this courtroom has to be used for another case this afternoon so we will adjourn now. Would you please return to this courtroom tomorrow morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will then be examined by the counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1.45 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 23rd day of May, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
